title: Why this is hard — and why that isn't a flaw
summary: The struggle is a sign of how your brain learned, not of weak willpower.

blocks.text: If quitting were just a matter of deciding, you'd have done it already. The fact that it's hard doesn't mean something is wrong with you — it means a very old part of your brain learned that this behaviour reliably delivers relief.
A learned loop, not a moral failing

Compulsive behaviours are habits stamped in by repetition. Each time the loop runs — trigger, behaviour, relief — the pathway gets a little stronger. That's learning working exactly as designed, just pointed at something that no longer serves you.
You are not fighting a lack of willpower. You're re-training a well-practised habit. Different problem, different tools.
What this means for you

items: Slips are information about the loop, not proof you can't change.
Small, repeated wins re-wire the pathway more than one heroic effort.
Self-criticism strengthens the very stress the loop feeds on.

title: Your brain on the dopamine loop
summary: Dopamine is about wanting, not liking — which is why urges outlast enjoyment.

blocks.text: Dopamine gets called the 'pleasure chemical', but that's not quite right. It's better understood as the 'wanting' or anticipation chemical. It spikes before the reward — driving you toward it — more than during it.
Why the wanting outlasts the liking

With a strong, always-available, endlessly-novel stimulus, the wanting system gets over-trained while the liking often fades. That gap — big urge, small actual satisfaction — is the trap many people describe: chasing something that stopped delivering a while ago.
The urge is real. The promised payoff is mostly a memory the wanting-system keeps quoting.
The good news

The same system that learned the loop can un-learn it. Every urge you ride out without acting teaches the wanting-system that the cue no longer predicts the reward. This is called extinction, and it's how the brain turns the volume down over time.

title: Urges are waves, not commands
summary: An urge rises, peaks, and falls on its own — usually within minutes.

blocks.text: It can feel like an urge will keep climbing until you give in. It won't. Urges follow a curve: they rise, crest, and fall — usually within a few minutes if you don't feed them with attention or fight them with panic.
Surfing instead of struggling
Urge surfing means noticing the wave and letting it move through you without acting on it. You're not white-knuckling it away; you're observing it, breathing, and letting the crest pass.

items: Name it: 'This is an urge. It will peak and pass.'
Locate it in your body and breathe into that spot.
Delay, don't forbid: 'Not now — I'll check back in 10 minutes.'

blocks.text: Every wave you ride teaches your brain the urge doesn't have to be obeyed. That's the rep that counts.

title: Why one slip snowballs — and how to stop it
summary: The abstinence-violation effect turns a slip into a spiral. You can interrupt it.

blocks.text: There's a well-studied pattern in recovery called the abstinence-violation effect. A single slip triggers a wave of shame and all-or-nothing thinking — 'I've blown it, so I may as well keep going' — and that thought, not the slip, is what causes the real damage.
The slip is a comma, not a full stop

One lapse doesn't erase your progress. The skills you built, the days you showed up, the pathway you weakened — those are still there. A slip is a single data point, best met with curiosity: what led here, and what would help next time?
That's why this app never resets your progress to zero. Your day-counter restarts, but your recovery score barely moves — because what you built is still yours.
If you slip

items: Pause the spiral: 'One slip is not a relapse.'
Get curious, not cruel: what was the trigger?
Take one small recovery action now, however small.

title: Rewiring: what recovery actually changes
summary: Sensitivity, mood, and motivation tend to recover as the loop quiets.

blocks.text: As you step out of the loop, many people notice a gradual return of things the loop had dulled: steadier mood, more motivation for ordinary rewards, better focus, and renewed interest in real-world connection.
This isn't instant, and it isn't linear — there are flat days and even harder days early on (sometimes called a 'flatline'). That's the system recalibrating, not proof it isn't working.
Recovery is less about white-knuckling forever and more about letting your baseline reset so ordinary life feels rewarding again.

title: Rebuilding intimacy and connection
summary: Recovery is a chance to move toward real closeness, not just away from a habit.

blocks.text: Recovery isn't only about stopping something — it's about making room for something better. Real intimacy is built on presence, honesty, and vulnerability, and those are skills you can practise.
Small moves toward connection

items: Name a feeling out loud to someone you trust.
Give full attention to one conversation today — phone away.
Let yourself be seen: share a real struggle, not just a highlight.

blocks.text: If shame has kept you isolated, connection is both the harder path and the more healing one.

title: Build a life bigger than the habit
summary: You don't just subtract a behaviour — you add a life that competes with it.

blocks.text: Willpower alone leaves a vacuum. The most durable recovery fills the space the habit used to occupy with things that genuinely matter to you: people, purpose, movement, creativity, rest.
Ask what the behaviour was really doing for you — soothing stress, killing boredom, numbing loneliness — and build healthier ways to meet that same need. That's what makes the change stick.
The goal isn't a smaller life without the habit. It's a fuller life that leaves less room for it.

title: A story: 90 days, one slip, and finishing anyway
summary: A composite account of what a realistic, non-perfect recovery can look like.

blocks.text: This is a composite story, drawn from common experiences rather than one person, to show what a realistic path can look like — messy, non-linear, and still successful.

The first two weeks were the hardest. Sleep was off, motivation flat, and the urges came in loud at night. Logging them — just naming each one — slowly made them feel smaller. Day 30 felt like a milestone; day 45 felt boring, which turned out to be a good sign.

Then, on day 62, a slip. The old voice said 'you've ruined it.' But instead of spiralling, there was a reflection: it was late, alone, doom-scrolling, stressed about work. Not a mystery — a pattern. The day-counter restarted; the progress didn't vanish.
The finish line was never 'perfect'. It was 'kept going after the slip'. That's the version that lasts.
